children: Raw sugar futures on ICE hit a fresh 16-month high on Wednesday as concerns about Indian supply and the Brazilian harvest increased, while arabica coffee sank to a five-week low.
SUGAR
* Raw sugar
​​settled up 0.34 cent, or 1.9%, at 18.70 cents per lb after climbing 3.1% on Tuesday. The market hit the highest price since April 2025 during the session at 18.77 cents.

* Dealers said tight supplies and strong domestic prices in top consumer India helped to fuel the recent run-up in prices, along with the prospect of lower production in the European Union and Thailand.

* One Indian trader said the request by the government that mills start the harvest earlier, to improve domestic supplies and reduce price pressure, might hurt yields since crops are not completely mature.
* In top producer Brazil, there is  (1.97 inches) of precipitation in the next 10 days for the main Ribeirao Preto sugarcane area, which should halt harvesting operations.
* White sugar
rose 1% to $539.20 a metric ton.
COFFEE
* Arabica coffee
settled down 11.35 cents, or 3.7%, at $2.981 per lb after hitting a five-week low of $2.9535.
* Dealers said there had been a pick-up in exports from Brazil as the harvest nears its end, helping to ease short-term supply tightness.

* "Higher prices over the last two weeks combined with the winding down of harvest brought differentials in Brazil to attractive levels for exporters," said Sucafina quantitative trader Ilya Byzov in a note.
"Additional exporter buying means additional futures hedging, which brings pressure on the market," he said.

* Cooxupe, Brazil's largest coffee cooperative, said on Wednesday that its farmers had harvested 91.9% of their 2026 crop by August 28, up from 87.5% a week earlier but lagging the 94.9% at the same point last year.
* Robusta coffee
lost 1.6% to $3,406 a ton, after hitting a 2-1/2-month low of $3,381.
COCOA
* London cocoa
settled down £238, or 4.9%, to £4,579 per ton. The market had risen to a one-year high of £4,988 on Tuesday.
* Dealers said there may still be a global surplus despite an expected decline in production in top grower Ivory Coast in the 2026/27 season that started this week.
* "We expect the global cocoa surplus to narrow sharply from 442,000 tons in 2025/26 to 82,000 tons in 2026/27, underpinning a firmer price floor," BMI analysts said in a note on Wednesday.
* Ample cocoa stockpiles should help to cushion any hit to global production from adverse weather, a Mondelez International executive said on Wednesday.
* New York cocoa
lost 4.5% to $6,273 a ton.
